item.title: Ducati's candidates to replace Marquez
item.author: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded: The shock news that Marc Marquez will call it quits on MotoGP at the end of this weekend creates a massive dilemma for Ducati, as it now tries to figure out exactly how to replace its star rider only days after he clinched another title success for the team and with 2027 testing about to begin.Not since Jorge Lorenzo dramatically retired at the end of the 2019 season has a factory team had to find a new racer at the final round of the season, but it’s fair to say that the retirement of Marquez will create substantially more ripples through the grand prix paddock than his former rival’s did.The most obvious solution, of course, is that Ducati promotes one of the rest of its line-up and, given the support and trust that Ducati Corse boss Gigi Dall’Igna has placed in since signing him as a then-rookie on a four-year MotoGP deal, it’s hard to imagine that it would be anyone else right now. That will create a vacancy at the VR46 team Aldeguer is currently scheduled to ride for next season.Go beyond the headlines and sign up to The Lean Angle, The Race's MotoGP newsletter. You'll get bespoke content direct to your inbox every Tuesday, plus the occasional one-off edition like today, where we had a special on the Marquez retirement news. The only other obvious contender is VR46's other 2027 signing: reigning World Superbike champion and 2027 MotoGP rookie - and the decision between which of the two is likely to get the nod will probably be measured in something that only Ducati has access to: lap times from testing on the 850cc bikes being used next year.Aldeguer has already had a chance to jump onto next year’s factory bike, deputising for the departing Pecco Bagnaia at two post-race tests, but we’ve not heard much about how he performed in those closed-to-the-media outings at Brno and the Red Bull Ring.However, while Aldeguer has had his time on the 850, Bulega has essentially been the lead development rider for the project thanks to his WSBK position meaning he’s not held back by MotoGP’s testing restrictions - and the initial suggestions have been that he has been very, very fast indeed.Either way, though, the promotion of one of them to sit alongside Pedro Acosta in the most coveted seat in MotoGP will leave a space (ironically) at Valentino Rossi’s VR46 satellite team - a seat that might actually be harder to fill than Marquez’s.The obvious choice, of course is Spanish Moto2 championship contender Manu Gonzalez, who goes into this weekend’s final race with a slender 4.5 point lead over already-confirmed 2027 MotoGP rookie Izan Guevara - and who many feel like has already been overlooked for a premier class seat for the past two seasons.He already has limited MotoGP experience after standing in for Ai Ogura at Trackhouse Aprilia for a post-race test last year, and he certainly didn’t embarrass himself there. And while he’s already renewed with his IntactGP team for Moto2 next year, most contracts have a MotoGP escape clause - that is, after all, how Alex Marquez ended up joining his brother Marc at Repsol Honda in 2020, when he replaced Lorenzo.One name that deserves to be in the conversation, of course, is this weekend's second factory Ducati rider , who has completed a number of very impressive MotoGP stand-in rides this year alongside his World Superbike duties.However, he might have created a cross for his own back with a strong run of form as Bulega's number two this season, with Ducati's production bike hopes now resting firmly on his shoulders for 2027.Of course, there’s an argument for helping one of the current MotoGP refugees find a spot for next year instead, with race winners such as and without a ride as things stand right now - but that will likely be a question decided on whether Ducati wants to invest in future potential, or is just looking for a one-year seat filler before is can settle things longer term during 2027.That option might be interesting to the team, though, because it disrupts MotoGP’s two-year contract cycle a little - and potentially even opens the door to Marquez’s protege finding his way onto the MotoGP grid a little earlier than initially expected.There’s a very short timeline on making those decisions, though, because Ducati will absolutely want its new rider, whoever it is, to make their debut for the factory next Tuesday at the post-race test, so that it can start the process of moulding them into a MotoGP racer sooner rather than later.

item.title: F1 drivers go through quizzical exercise in stewarding debate
Influencers rejoice: The follow-me camera drone that can fly at 25mph and fits in your jersey pocket is now on sale
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: Capturing drone footage of yourself riding used to mean having someone else on hand to fly the drone, or dangerously attempting to control one yourself while riding. Whether you're a budding infuencer or want to capture rides with your mates for a bit of fun, the HOVERAir X1 PROMAX self-flying drone makes it much easier to get those shots. The X1 PROMAX is HOVERAir's flagship self-flying action camera, capable of automatically tracking riders across a wide range of situations and capturing footage in up to 8K resolution. Better still, its compact design means it slips easily into a cycling jersey pocket so you can have it ready whenever you want to capture a shot.It's a premium bit of kit, but these Black Friday deals in the UK and US make it considerably more tempting.The X1 PROMAX is an excellent option if you want a drone you can stash in your jersey pocket and make great cycling video content. It can keep up with you while riding, and is smart enough to avoid lowhanging branches when riding off-road.View DealThis is the brand's flagship follow-me drone, making it an ideal companion for capturing your adventures, particularly when you're riding on your own. View DealWe've found HOVERAir drones very easy to use. Once connected to the app, you simply select your preferred flight mode and distance, launch the drone and start riding. The different flight modes offer plenty of options, too. Dolly Track allows the drone to fly backwards while keeping you in frame, while Follow Me mode tracks your movements automatically. Tracking performance is impressive, with the X1 ProMax capable of following riders through woodland and keeping up with faster efforts. It can track at speeds of up to 42km/h, with short bursts of up to 60km/h.When you're finished, simply hold out your hand and the drone will return and land in your palm. Weighing just 192g, it can then be folded away and slipped into a jersey pocket, so there's no need to carry any extra luggage.The price mentioned here is for the standard HOVERAir X1 ProMax package, but there are also discounts available on several bundles through the HOVERAir website, which include additional accessories to help you get more out of the drone.If you're interested in trying out a self-flying camera but don't want to spend quite as much, the older HOVERAir X1 is also worth considering. As the predecessor to the PROMAX, it doesn't offer the same 8K capabilities, but it retains the convenient follow-me functionality in a similarly compact design. It's currently 15% off, down to £228.

item.title: Our verdict on Marc Marquez's bombshell MotoGP retirement
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: Marc Marquez dropped a huge bombshell as the final MotoGP round of the season kicked off at Valencia by announcing he is retiring from racing after this weekend.Here's our take on the decision.Who can blame him? Going out on topThere have been suggestions for weeks that Marc would retire at the end of the season, but it’s absolutely worth stressing this: almost none of them have come from inside the MotoGP paddock, with nearly everyone that you speak to (including people very much inside the Marquez inner circle) almost certain that he would continue on.There was, so went the belief, still so much to come. New regulations for next year, and the chance to do what he’s never done and win on a different spec of bike. The opportunity to give us the moment Casey Stoner denied us, and test himself against his hotshot new Ducati team-mate Pedro Acosta.Instead, he’s walked away - and honestly, after countless surgeries, dozens of broken bones, and 10 world titles, who can blame him? He’s going out on top, on his own terms.What it says about his 2026 titleMy apologies for bringing Formula 1 into this - I will keep it short. I remember being a fresh-faced editorial assistant when Nico Rosberg dropped his retirement announcement on us in 2016, and while those memories are so incredibly distinct (at home versus on track, new to the industry versus much more settled), the vision of it all is surprisingly similar.When Rosberg got his one F1 title over the line, it was knife-edge. We all knew - he probably knew, too - that this was the one and only. He clearly accepted that quickly and was happy to leave it at that.Marquez has won eight in MotoGP, but this is the first one he's won in this way. This is the first one that felt truly knife-edge, that felt lost and then found, that felt like it was taking more out of him than ever before and something different out of him than before.He points-raced to it, with just a handful of crashes from his return at Mugello six months ago to now, whereas normally he was the one leading the crash standings. This time he played the odds and the opponent, and had to convince his body - the much-suffering arm, the diminished shoulder - to play along.I have little doubt he could have won again. But I genuinely believe he no longer liked the odds, and could no longer justify to himself all the physical travails that would continue to be required to maintain those odds.This adds to the legacy of his 2026 title, that I for so long didn't believe in. It was such a tightrope act that it's made the greatest rider in MotoGP history go 'OK, that was crazy - crazy enough to call it a day'.Absolutely the right decision but a huge 2027 lossGiven everything his body has been through, everything he has achieved, this is absolutely the right moment for Marc Marquez to retire. He has nothing more to prove and there is no point risking yet more injuries. Totally, totally the right call.But I am so, so, so gutted that we will now never get to see how him versus Acosta in the same team would have panned out.Stoner's shock retirement months before Marquez arrived in MotoGP deprived us of one epic head to head, but was totally the right call for Stoner.Now Marquez has deprived us of something that would have been even more epic.But good for him. He's picked his moment perfectly.The greatest I have ever seenI'll keep it short and sweet: he has earned this moment. The amount of pain, suffering and ability to keep coming back again and again has finally taken its toll on him.He retired on his terms, something that he may have thought might not have been possible just a few months ago with the state of his right arm. To win his 1oth world title through sheer mental strength and earn the right to be called the greatest motorcycle rider of all time is the perfect ending.The greatest I have ever seen, what a pleasure it has been.Stops any doubt about GOAT statusMarc Marquez's bombshell retirement will cement him as MotoGP's Greatest of All Time.He was already that in my view - he's beaten many of MotoGP's other GOAT contenders to his first titles, and then won more after completing one of sport's great injury comebacks post-Jerez 2020 (and all the setbacks that followed).But retiring now on his own terms ensures that nothing that happens in 2027 will change that.Acosta was the only rider who I felt would have half a chance against Marquez on the same bike, and now Marquez won't be going head-to-head with him.Had Marquez tripped up there - something not out of the question, given he'd have to adapt to a whole new formula and Acosta's enormous potential - that may have put an asterisk over his status as the GOAT.Instead, Marquez has left the building and leaves behind a scrap to be MotoGP's new benchmark rider, a fight I wouldn't be surprised if his Ducati successor wins.From a selfish point of view as an observer and fan of MotoGP, I don't want Marc to stop. But I get why it's happening. The mission is complete.He's been through hell since 2020, fought back to the top of the mountain, got hurt a few more times along the way, and after dominating 2025 pulled off an unthinkable comeback in 2026.What else is there left to achieve? How many more times should he risk destroying his body just because his presence in MotoGP is box office?Of course I'd have loved to see him up against Acosta on equal machinery. But we'll just have to add that to the long list of epic head-to-heads we've narrowly missed out on in many forms of motorsport dating back decades.Marquez has carried MotoGP on his shoulders for long enough. Those shoulders deserve a break, and now it's time for new stars to lead the series into its Liberty-owned era. Who's going to step up?I expected to be making a coffee at the start of FP1, not watching the greatest MotoGP rider of all time announcing his retirement on some slides.Taking a step back, this shouldn’t really be as shocking as it is, and yet we’re all speechless. This is a man whose body has been battered by countless injuries and surgeries over his career, but especially the last six years. This was a championship which came from 102 points back after yet more injury.He’s now stepping away at the very top of his game, coming back from years of turmoil to reclaim his crown - not just once, but twice.It is, of course, a shame that we won’t see Marquez vs Acosta, that much awaited battle between the king and the heir.But whatever happens, it is beyond doubt now that Marc Marquez did it better than anyone else.Blah blah blah, yeah yeah yeah… but ten.He's never seemed so physically spentFriday’s FP1 is usually a lower key ambience to kick off the weekend. But the eerie silence as the camera cut to Marc Marquez let us know something was up. Ever the maestro of conducting the media off track, it was simple but utterly shocking to read the words 'This will be my last race in MotoGP'. I expected a playful '…for 2026' to follow on a final card, but no. This is the end - mercifully, on track, on his own terms.We will not see Marc on the next generation of MotoGP bikes. There will be no Honda reunion and no head to head with Pedro Acosta as Ducati’s newest prince in waiting. There will not be an 11th world championship title. But for all the tantalising future narratives we lose, what an extraordinary chapter of MotoGP history we have witnessed. The talent hasn’t diminished, the mind is sharper than ever, but the injuries have now clearly taken a toll too far to continue. Reflecting on his 2026 season, Marc has never seemed so physically spent after his sessions, so there is a logic to this timing. The 1000cc chapter closes, he has given everything, leaving this extraordinary sport battled-scarred but having made an impact as one of the true legends of motorcycle racing.Someone give Gigi Dall’igna a hug, he’s had an emotional 24 hours.Robs us of tantalising Acosta battle in 2027In many ways, Marquez’s retirement makes sense: he arguably has nothing more to achieve, his body is already broken enough, and a retirement on his own terms is nothing less than he deserves.I feel quite sentimental about the end of this chapter though. Hearing Marquez’s story about his attempted comeback in Jerez after that 2020 crash is what got me into MotoGP. Following along with his journey back from all of those injuries and struggles at Honda to his successes with Ducati has been incredible to watch.He’s also cemented his status as the greatest of all time in my book, especially over the last two season. Could he have won again in 2027? I think so, but that’s something only he knows for sure.So happy to have witnessed the (tail-end) of a stellar career and happy that he can end it this way. That being said, I’m slightly annoyed that we’ve been robbed of what could have been blockbuster battles between Marquez and Acosta at Ducati in 2027, and also extremely curious about what comes next.I pity the first 'after-Marc' world championI sort of pity the first A.M. (after Marc) MotoGP world champion...My main disappointment is we won't see if anyone could have properly overthrown him.He'd so emphatically reminded everybody he was the best in the business that maybe he wouldn't have been beaten, of course. It'll just feel slightly hollow for whoever succeeds him as world champion because justifiably or not there'll probably be that little asterisk of 'well, he only won because Marc stopped'. I'm trying to consider a hypothetical F1 alternative that fits better than the obvious comparison of Nico Rosberg in 2016. Rosberg was world champion but he wasn't the best driver in F1 at the time. So he couldn't be 'dethroned,' but I don't think there was an overarching 'ah, man, it would have been good to see who could have beat him' at play there. With Marquez you know that MotoGP's losing the absolute benchmark. Go beyond the headlines and sign up to The Lean Angle, The Race's MotoGP newsletter. You'll get bespoke content direct to your inbox every Tuesday, plus the occasional one-off edition like today, where we had a special on the Marquez retirement news.

item.title: Volvo's big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
item.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.content:encoded: COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015, both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric. As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market. At the same time, Europe and China electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets.So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base.Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before.

item.title: Yankees news: Catcher market is already drying up

item.content:encoded: NY Post | Mark W. Sánchez: The Yankees are open to bringing in a catcher, especially if he’s a good defender behind the plate and hits from the right side. They may need to hurry up, though, because the market might be drying up: Tyler Stephenson returned to the Reds, Gary Sánchez committed his future to the Marlins, and Ryan Jeffers accepted the Twins’ qualifying offer. Sánchez goes through some of the Yanks’ remaining options, including Carson Kelly, Austin Hedges, Kyle Higashioka, and more.Heavy: Jonathan Loáisiga agreed to sign a two-year deal with the Yankees this week. As it turns out, according to New York Post’s Jon Heyman, the reliever actually turned down a more lucrative offer from the Mets to return to the Bronx.NY Post | Greg Joyce: With Paul Goldschmidt signing a one-year deal with the Mets, he wraps up a productive two-year stint with the Yankees. The veteran first baseman revealed the reasons why he decided to move in a different direction. “My top concern was not, ‘Hey, how do I go to someplace where I get the most playing time?’ ” Goldschmidt said Wednesday morning. “My concern was going to a team where it felt right … and just have an opportunity to be on a team that has a chance to win and is going for it. Obviously, the Mets are in that.” The former NL MVP will likely platoon with Jared Young at first base in Queens.MLB.com | Thomas Harrigan: Harrigan takes a look at the Yankees’ bullpen heading into 2027: signings already made, unsigned free agents, and where the unit stands at this moment, a few days until the looming lockout starts on Dec. 1.

item.title: Game Preview: Knicks vs. Heat, November 27, 2026
item.author: Moritz Wollert
item.content:encoded: Back in the 1990s, one way to preserve basketball games for the future was to record them on a VHS cassette. For all the younger folks, this was a big, chunky, rectangular thing that had magnetic tape on the inside. Whenever a game was on TV, you popped your cassette into the video recorder, pressed “REC,” and from that point on, you could rewatch anything you recorded whenever you wanted. Or for as long as the tape held up, for that matter.My favorite recorded event back then was Game Five of the first round of the playoffs in 1999 between your New York Knicks and the Miami Heat. It ended with Allan Houston’s historic leaning jumper with 0.8 seconds to go, sending the top-seeded team coached by the Godfather of Schenectady packing and the underdog Bockers on an improbable run all the way to the NBA Finals. The tape wasn’t just special to me because of the historic shot or the basketball played with bad intentions back then. It was also awesome because it showed the Knicks beating the Heat. Sorry, Grandma, I know you taught me not to hate anyone, but those were the Heat, my favorite team’s biggest rival for years.Now, before A’ja Wilson’s boyfriend thinks he can hold a candle to the guy Patrick Ewing once offered one of his kidneys to, let me make it clear: That was a different time, a different rivalry. Whoever experienced it firsthand knows what I mean by that. When the Knicks meet the Heat on Friday night for their fourth NBA Cup game of the season, it will be different, much different. Different players, different coaches. Heck, it all seems like a different world. But make no mistake about it—it’s still Knicks versus Heat. Which means the stakes are just a bit higher than in a game versus the magicians from the nation’s capital or the royalty from “The Big Tomato.”Knicks get first look at Giannis on the HeatFriday’s game will be particularly interesting because it gives the Knicks a first glimpse at the newest version of the Heat, featuring Greece’s national hero Giannis Antetokounmpo, who also happens to be one of the greatest and probably most unique basketball players this generation has seen. The project started pretty badly, with Giannis continuously reminding everyone who cared and everyone who didn’t that he dearly missed Milwaukee, the city he had called home for every second of his storied NBA career until then. Then the schematic issues befell the not-so-hot Heat, who struggled with spacing, players playing in new roles, and the daunting task of implementing a headstrong player with immense gravity into a completely new system. Defense? Haha, good one!But after a 3-6 start, the second-oldest team in the league decided this wasn’t the way to ride off into the sunset. Or rather, their famous coach made plenty of adjustments. Erik Spoelstra, as we all know, is one of the best in the business. Not only at taking average rosters into the Play-In Tournament but indeed at coaching that sport with the orange leather. He inserted young Pelle Larsson into the starting lineup, found a spacing solution for the Heat, doubled down on their identity as a full-court, offensive-minded team, and then watched his guys reel off seven mostly impressive victories in a row (among them wins over Houston and Detroit) before falling to Philly on Wednesday night.What can we expect from the Heat specifically? They love to get up and down the court and play at the third-highest pace in the entire league. Currently, only the Memphis Grizzlies score more points than Spoelstra’s squad, and the Heat do it by shooting a high percentage from the field, drawing boatloads of fouls, and making use of two post players. Yes, you read that right—post players. Both Giannis and A’ja Wilson’s boyfriend can effectively score with their backs to the basket, and despite many worries, they can actually coexist next to one another. One of them fills the dunker spot almost all the time, they rotate decisively in screen actions, and overall, Miami runs its sets fast and ferociously to get them rolling downhill. They don’t just set screens to see where it leads them; they want to get into an action quickly before any lanes can close.Heat, Spoelstra have adjusted after bad startIt works, partly because the players around Giannis and that guy who made a habit last year of disliking the team that won a championship before him are all doing a good job in their roles. Klay Thompson adds shooting (43.2 percent from downtown), Swedish Swiss Army knife Pelle Larsson provides a little bit of everything, and playmaker Davion Mitchell has all of a sudden turned into one of the better point guards in the league at age 28, averaging career highs of 17 points and 8.6 assists per contest while also shooting 51 percent from the floor and 43-plus percent from behind the arc. The bench has some older vets more or less collecting paychecks so far, but Bobby Portis and Andrew Wiggins clearly have some talent. Apparently, that also describes Ryan Conwell, a stocky second-round guard who has been a pleasant surprise for Miami.That whole group will definitely look to waltz into Madison Square Garden on Friday with the idea of showing the champs that they are a team to be reckoned with. Whether they truly are remains to be seen; there are plenty of things that could uproot the positivity currently sprawling across South Beach. But the Knicks better be prepared for a tough test, and not because they might still be missing some of their injured guys or because they are coming off an emotionally draining victory against Cleveland on Wednesday. Not even because A’ja Wilson might have taught her boyfriend a few more tricks this offseason after winning her fifth WNBA MVP trophy.No, it’s going to be tough because it’s Heat versus Knicks. And even if that doesn’t mean what it did in the days of the VHS cassette, it still means something.Who: Miami Heat (10-7) at New York Knicks (12-6)Date: Friday, November 27, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, New York, NYFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

item.content:encoded: Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against BrentfordNottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded. item.author: Donald McRae
item.content:encoded: Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts“I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil. Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United, whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.Continue reading...

item.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
item.author: David Batty
item.content:encoded: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers MuseumIn 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.Continue reading...

item.title: Your chance to ask Michael Matthews anything about professional cycling, his career and more – AskCN
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: Our next reader Q&A is here! This time you can pose your questions not just to our team, but to an actual current pro, Australia's Michael Matthews.We're going to catch up with Matthews next week at the Jayco AlUla team camp, and we're going to ask him exclusively YOUR questions for the next instalment of our series.Now in his 18th year as a professional, Matthews has had a rollercoaster season to say the least, starting the year with a win before suffering a nasty crash that saw him break both his arms. Impressively, the 36-year-old came back for the Tour de France, where he was regularly in breakaways, and has packed in lots of racing in the latter part of the season, perhaps catching up for lost time.Next year, he will race for Jayco AlUla once more, where he remains one of their top riders and someone who can excel on all types of terrain.As a veteran of the peloton, Matthews knows the ins and outs of the sport and its politics, especially how it's changed over the last two decades, and how riders like him have to evolve with the rapidly changing nature of the sport.So whether your question is about his long-running career, his goals for the future, or just what it's like in the peloton at the moment, we're sure Matthews will be able to answer anything and everything you want to know – so get thinking!You can drop your questions in the comments below, email us at engagement@cyclingnews.com, or leave a comment on our social media channels. We'll be publishing the answers next week, and we'll endeavour to let you know if your question has been answered.Remember: everyone and anyone can submit a question, but the Q&A will be exclusively for our subscribers, so make sure you're signed up if you want to see the answers – plus our Labs testing, expert columns, in-depth interviews and investigations, and much more. item.title: Is this cycling’s ‘Moneyball’ moment? Inside the arms race for UCI points
item.author: James Witts
item.content:encoded: "After my presentation in Barcelona, teams wanted to chat and compare their models with mine. This is a growing field, whether it's in search of points or simply improving performance as a whole." That's Louis Van Gaelen. The Belgian's undertaking a PhD in health and artificial intelligence at the University of Antwerp. As a side project, the keen cyclist dug deep into professional cycling and, as his presentation at this year's Science & Cycling Conference revealed, 'roster optimisation for maximal UCI points'. It's not the sexiest of titles, but Van Gaelen's hobby, aligned with the work of an increasing number of data scientists around the sport, is proving critical for not only a team's success but their survival. It's time to talk about the merits of not aiming for victory…How does the system work?The current UCI promotion and relegation system, rolled out in 2020, works in three-year cycles with 18 licences available to the men's WorldTour. The Women's WorldTour has 15 licences; however, demand for these spots is less competitive due to the limited number of teams willing to make the step up. The 2026 season was the first season in the latest cycle, meaning points earned up to the end of 2028 will determine the WorldTour line-up for 2029 to 2031. "All points from UCI-sanctioned races count towards the team total, but only the points accrued from the top-20 scoring riders," Van Gaelen adds. "Remaining at WorldTour can make or break a team."That's because WorldTour status guarantees teams entry into cycling's biggest races, including the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España. Relegation means losing automatic invitations, reducing television exposure, sponsor value and commercial income. It also makes attracting top riders harder, potentially creating a vicious circle of declining competitiveness. The UCI also assesses a team's non-sporting side, including the financial stability of the team, which is why they granted Team Picnic PostNL a truncated 12-month licence for 2026. At the time of the ruling, the Dutch team hadn't finalised medium- to long-term backing with one of its sponsors, leaving the required fiscal guarantees for 2027 and 2028 incomplete. The Picnic turbulence continues to this day, heightened by serious allegations about team culture, with December 8, 2026 a key date in the calendar, as that's when the UCI is expected to confirm 2027 registrations.But let's return to sporting criteria, as that's why the likes of Van Gaelen are in demand. His work looked to answer which riders a team should sign; which races each rider should participate in; and how a team can maximise its total UCI points across a season. The search involved combining two technologies: machine learning and mathematical optimisation.Machine learning utilised 10 seasons' worth of data, covering thousands of riders and their previous performances, in addition to race profiles and course difficulty. "Inputting the course profiles was a laborious job," Van Gaelen says. "It involved uploading many, many course GPX files from an internet forum." Van Gaelen's machine-learning model then predicted the likely finishing order of riders in individual races, which were translated into expected UCI points using the relevant race's points scale. The second part, mathematical optimisation, aimed to build the perfect roster by, for instance, matching climbers and sprinters to races where they're likeliest to score, by reducing clashes between teammates and setting a race-day ceiling at 85 days."With our optimised roster and focusing on one team in particular, we increased the points per rider from an average of 375.3 to 824.7," Van Gaelen explains. "Of course, there are limitations – our model didn't take into account fatigue, for example – but it's a promising proof of concept."If Van Gaelen's work is good on paper, XDS Astana's is good in practice. The Kazakh team are the poster boys for optimising rosters in search of UCI points. At the end of the 2024 season, they were facing almost certain relegation, languishing 21st in the annual UCI rankings. But that's when they made one of their most important signings of recent times: data scientist Morgan Saussine. One of the key implementations from Saussine's work was to prioritise top-10 finishes over individual victories. While historically teams would often organise their racing around one protected leader, with teammates sacrificing their own results to help that rider win, Saussine, who was unavailable for interview at the time of writing, identified there was much lower-hanging fruit to pick from in search of points.Astana set about assembling a squad capable of scoring across different race categories, terrains and stages of the season. Into the squad came 14 new faces, including experienced riders such as Wout Poels, Diego Ulissi, Fausto Masnada and Mike Teunissen. The arrival of Chinese sponsor XDS provided additional financial resources to support the change. It worked, as they shot up the rankings to finish fourth in 2025 and so preserve their WorldTour status. Cofidis went down."Given the situation XDS Astana faced at the beginning of the 2025 season, when the team urgently needed UCI points, it's easy to see why a rider like Christian Scaroni was so invaluable," says researcher Simon Lucat. "Here's a rider who regularly finishes in the top-10 across a demanding race calendar."Scaroni's importance to the cause was also highlighted this season with the 29-year-old Italian finishing inside the top-10 of one-day races or stages 33 times. He also won the overall at the Tour of Oman.Lucat, a lifelong cycling fan and an economics student at Bocconi University in Milan, Italy, researched the inherent paradox that is professional cycling: results are attributed to individual riders, but they're collectively produced by a team."One of the main findings of my research is that the combined quality of the riders surrounding the leader can be just as important as the quality of the leader himself when it comes to accumulating UCI points," he says. "Strong teammates are valuable not only because they can help the leader achieve a better result, but also because they can score points themselves.""The balance may also depend on the type of race," he adds. "Paris-Roubaix, for example, stood out in my analysis as a race where squad depth appeared to be particularly important. This makes sense if you think about the nature of the race, where a puncture or a crash can completely change a team's plans. Having several competitive riders gives you more options."The original points detectiveThe likes of Van Gaelen and Lucat are building on the foundations laid by Raul Banqueri. In 2020, the diligent Spaniard waded through the UCI's 400-page road-racing regulations PDF in search of content for his Twitter account. It was needle-in-a-haystack stuff, but he pricked his fingers when he unearthed what many had missed. "I saw the UCI had started using sporting criteria to award licences and distribute wildcards to the WorldTour calendar," he says, "but almost nobody was reporting on it." He did, piquing the public's interest. And that of the professionals."When I started publishing my analyses of the points system, a multitude of WorldTour sports directors, performance directors and cyclists started following me on Twitter," he says. "Then in 2023 I started working with the Human Powered Health women's team. That season their licence was at risk, so I prepared a dashboard with advanced statistics on results and UCI points. We thoroughly analysed the calendar to identify which races they could score the most points in with the roster they had. The team focused more on flat races and minor races, tripled their UCI points compared to 2022 (from 914 to 3354) and managed to save their WorldTour licence. "Nowadays, UCI points are no longer as important in women's cycling, as there aren't enough teams applying for the licence, but the dashboard remains valuable for the scouting process, signings and monitoring team performance."That year, he also collaborated on projects with Visma-Lease a Bike, assisting the team's head of strategy, Patrick Broe, while in 2025 he saddled up with the Movistar Team women's squad, helping with data and video analysis. In short, Banqueri is hot property when it comes to delivering peak points and peak performance. So, what's his assessment of sniffing out peak points performers?"Sprinters capable of getting over hills or specialists in hilly races with high top speed are increasingly sought after to claim points," he answers. "That includes Benoît Cosnefroy, Thomas Silva, Alex Aranburu, Natnael Tesfatsion and Lukáš Kubiš, who've all scored good points for their respective teams.""In general, one-day races are significantly more profitable than stage races," he adds. "One-day races award the same points as the general classification of a race in the same category, and stages award very few points, except in the Grand Tours. Right now, I believe that ProSeries one-day races (250 points for the winner) are the most profitable in terms of UCI points."Banqueri says an interesting development is the strategy and recruitment adopted by ProTeams, whose goal is the top 30 of the annual ranking in search of an invite to the Grand Tours. "These teams are the ones looking the most for races outside of Europe, especially in Asia, where the level is lower, since they can score a high percentage of their total seasonal UCI points. For WorldTeams, it's less profitable to travel to race in Asia, as it causes huge fatigue for their cyclists, and the UCI points they earn don't have as much impact on their total sum of UCI points."Also, some of the lower-level ProTeams, like Burgos BH, have signed cyclists from more immature cycling nations to take advantage of the UCI points they can win in National Championships and Continental Championships. All Continental Championships award the same points, as do National Championships, provided the nation participated in the previous World Championships. So, being the champion of Mauritius scores the same points as being the champion of France." To that end, five of Burgos BH's eight 2025 wins came at the national championships of Mauritius, plus Uruguay, Guatemala, Mongolia and Greece. In 2026, it was three from nine wins."In both seasons, the Spanish outfit finished comfortably in the top-30, essentially guaranteeing them a wildcard spot at the Vuelta a España. These wildcard spots are keenly fought over for the same reasons that teams strain to cling onto WorldTour status, namely media exposure and sponsor value.Downside of chasing pointsFor ProTeams, this short-term points grab could have long-term consequences for the sport. "This year, Bardiani had the lowest average age (only 22.4 years, according to Pro Cycling Stats) and ultimately fell out of the top 30 in the ranking, meaning they won't be invited to the Giro d'Italia in 2027," says Banqueri. "It's a bit unfair because a team like Bardiani is essential for developing young cyclists. It means in the future they'll probably have to sign more experienced cyclists to ensure results."If there is a future. Come the end of the 2026 season, veteran team boss Bruno Reverberi couldn't contain his anger at the points system, calling the UCI "incompetent". Reverberi told the TriCiclo podcast that with no guarantees of invitation to the world's biggest races – they'd raced every Giro d'Italia since 1982 – they could soon be out of business. "How can you spend €5 million and not have the right to race? There is no future, and cycling has no future. We've already thought about closing in two years. In fact, we have taken four or five new riders and made them sign for only one year."The Italian team, who have nurtured the likes of Sonny Colbrelli and Giulio Pellizzari, are known for their attacking style. The UCI points system, Reverberi laments, is anti-cycling, encouraging top-10s rather than chasing glory in the breakaway. "The UCI is incompetent. They've destroyed cycling," he concluded.He's not the only critic of chasing lesser places rather than the podium. This is from Jayco Alula's Michael Matthews earlier in 2026: "For me it's destroying cycling." And this from Serge Parsani, team manager at ProTeam Solution Tech NIPPO Rail: "It's undoubtedly an anomalous ranking." EF Education-EasyPost boss Jonathan Vaughters went so far as to say that collecting UCI points was forcing teams to participate in too many smaller races, some of which had inadequate safety arrangements. "They're [riders] being pressured by team managers like me saying 'we've got to get points – hurry up.'"In short, a system designed to reward sporting performance ends up discouraging teams from racing to win. It's an imperfect system. This is the result of professional cycling's imperfect business model where teams are almost wholly reliant on sponsors for survival. It's one reason why 24 teams have recently formed the Collective Cycling Group (CCG), aimed at reforming the sport and streamlining the calendar. We'll no doubt hear more of the CCG in the near future, but it does highlight the fragility of cycling at the top level. Then again, which successful organisation doesn't look to optimise resources for maximum value? Back to Lucat…"I was also interested in the relationship between budget and team performance," he says. "You'd naturally expect wealthier teams to perform better because they can recruit stronger riders, but my findings suggest that differences in measured rider quality alone do not fully explain their advantage. A team's budget buys much more than just riders. Part of that advantage could come from better coaching, nutrition, equipment, medical support or logistics.""Smaller teams cannot match the spending of the biggest WorldTour teams, so they have to be very smart about how they use their resources, whether in recruitment, race selection or the composition of their line-ups," Lucat continues. "This is where data analysis could be especially valuable for teams that cannot simply rely on having the strongest riders in the peloton."In English football's top division, the three B's – Brighton and Hove Albion, Bournemouth and Brentford – are examples of sporting teams who have maximised data to punch above their collective weight. As Lucat says, if your budget is nominal, you must maximise every pound, dollar or euro. That said, one measure of success for every business is efficiency. Just look at UAE Team Emirates-XRG. Their budget is an estimated £50 million per year – the highest in professional road cycling – but for that they've not only nurtured arguably the greatest rider of all time and dominated the rankings, they also finished third in the 2026 WorldTour budget efficiency table, put together by the website 'How to turn pro', which tracks the fiscal side of professional cycling.Though we can't take the website's findings as gospel truth – they state that rider and team budgets are based on factors like the limited publicly available information – they do document sources, as well as featuring a public changelog and correction process.According to the site, the UAE squad accrued 656 points per £1 million spent in 2026. That was behind second-placed XDS Astana – 749 points per million from an estimated budget of £ 23 million – and the most efficient team, Uno-X Mobility, whose 784 points per million came from an overall estimated budget of £ 16.7 million.Keep scrolling, and you’ll upset Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his accountants, who continue to return very little on their sporting investments. Netcompany Ineos ranked 17th out of 18 in the efficiency stakes; their mooted £43.5 million resulted in just 300 points per million. Picnic were low on budget and efficiency – £16.7 million and 178 points per million – leaving them rock bottom.Looking ahead, if Picnic survive into 2027, they have some catching up to do, finishing this season with just 2,822 points. Groupama-FDJ are the next WorldTour team, over 6,500 points ahead on 9,329, followed by NSN Cycling (9,624 points). At the ProTeam level, Tom Pidcock's Pinarello-Q36.5 team (12th in rankings) and Tudor Pro Cycling (17th) are the leading contenders for promotion. Where does that leave us? All in all, professional cycling's points race has made data, recruitment and calendar planning essential tools of survival, not merely marginal gains. Yet when teams optimise for rankings rather than victories, the system risks distorting the sport it's meant to reward. As Banqueri signs off, this is sport where the ultimate victory is victory itself: "Of course, teams without a large budget must seek a balance between performing in the big races, which have a greater media impact, and scoring points in minor races that give them peace of mind in the rankings. But UCI points are not the only important metric of a team's success. Movistar finished the season in 13th position but won La Vuelta. Surely Astana would have traded their season for Movistar's?"

item.title: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
item.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.content:encoded:
Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win. Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy, and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41.“Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It's the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.” The video was directed by Zack Snyder and features Matt Damon’s voice-over.
Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura.

item.title: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? | Polly Toynbee

item.content:encoded: High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.”They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.”Continue reading...

item.title: Our top-rated cycling headphones are now 35% off – save on Sony's LinkBuds Clip in the US and UK
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: The best cycling headphones are among the few pieces of kit that see use both on the bike and off. However, that brings competing demands. Away from the bike, you may value features such as noise cancelling, but if you're looking for headphones to use whilst cycling, you are most likely after something that also allows you to hear your surroundings.That's where the Sony LinkBuds Clip come in. They've taken the top spot in our best headphones for cycling buying guide thanks to their fantastic sound quality and secure fit. They feature an open-ear design, which is essentially a small speaker that sits near, but crucially not in your ear, so you can enjoy your music or podcasts without blocking out the sounds around you.Whether you're looking for a pair for yourself or to pick up as a gift, the LinkBuds Clip are well worth considering. With 35% off in both the UK and the US, now is a great time to grab a pair. For US readers, the LinkBuds Clip are also available with 35% off, making now a great time to pick up our top-rated cycling headphones for less. Their open-ear design makes them particularly well suited to cycling and they're just as practical for everyday use.View DealThe LinkBuds Clip are a brilliant option that come into their own in busy riding environments. Their open-ear design allows you to hear traffic and other sounds around you, while remaining comfortable and unobtrusive. View DealThe LinkBuds Clip are a neat design, and they come with a small charging case that's easy to pocket in the event you suddenly find some company, or decide you've had enough of the podcast you're listening to. As for battery life, you get up to nine hours of playback with the earbuds and up to 28 hours with the charging case, giving you 37 hours in total. That's plenty for even the longest rides and multi-day adventures. Despite their looks, these headphones are unlikely to fall out and don't interfere with your riding glasses. They clip onto your ears rather than hooking over the top, which is very comfortable and unobtrusive. If you'd prefer something other than black, the earbuds are also available in green, greige and lavender.

item.title: 'When you see an opportunity, you have to act quickly' – Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand's cyclo-cross team find new sponsorship from 2027 onwards
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Sven Nys' cyclo-cross team has swiftly found a new title sponsor following the withdrawal of Glowi, owner of named sponsor Het Poetsbureau.The team, which is led by women's world champion Lucinda Brand and men's European champion Thibau Nys, welcomes electrical retailer Elektro Loeters as a new title sponsor alongside Baloise Verzekeringen.The new sponsorship will begin on January 1, 2027, though the length of the deal hasn't been announced."Elektro Loeters embodies the same winning mentality that we strive for every day," team manager Sven Nys said in an Instagram post announcing the news.The deal came about quickly, the team confirmed, with Elektro Loeters only approaching them in recent weeks."When you see an opportunity, you have to act quickly. We immediately felt a connection with the team’s vision and ambitions. Five days later, an agreement was already on the table. It shows just how similar entrepreneurship and top-level sport are."The team, currently known as Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions, have been the most successful during the 2026-27 cyclo-cross season so far with 12 victories.Nys has four wins, including three rounds of the X2O Trofee, while Brand has six, including two apiece in the X2O Trofee and Superprestige. Both triumphed at the UEC Cyclo-cross European Championships in Zeddam earlier this month.Like the team, Elektro Loeters is also experiencing success, with the company planning to open five new stores in Flanders in addition to its 10 pre-existing stores."Elektro Loeters embodies the same winning mentality that we strive for every day. Their growth story, entrepreneurial spirit and drive are a perfect match for our values. We are therefore looking forward to further developing this partnership over the coming months and putting it into action together," said Sven Nys.Brand and Thibau Nys will lead the team in their new identity alongside other key riders Pim Ronhaar and Annemarie Worst. However, this will be Brand's penultimate cyclo-cross season, as the Dutchwoman will retire from racing in April 2028.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Huge Black Friday discounts on Shimano road groupsets at Sigma Sports, with 105 Di2, Ultegra and Dura-Ace all better than half price
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: Shimano is one of cycling's biggest component brands, best known for its extensive range of groupsets covering road, gravel and mountain biking.The brand's range-topping Dura-Ace groupset delivers the highest level of road performance, with a race-proven design trusted at the biggest events in the world. Ultegra offers much of the same functionality at a lower price and with only a small weight penalty, making it a popular choice for performance-focused riders. Meanwhile, 105 brings electronic shifting to a more accessible price point, appealing to budget-conscious racers and endurance riders alike.Fortunately for UK shoppers, there's currently more than 50% off Shimano 12-speed Di2 road groupsets at Sigma Sports, covering everything from 105 to Dura-Ace. To suit a range of budgets and prices starting at just £699, there are some particularly good deals to be had here. Shimano's Dura-Ace, Ultegra and 105 groupsets are all 12-speed and feature electronic Di2 shifting, with a semi-wireless set-up across the range. Each offers a slightly different balance of weight, performance and price, but all are currently considerably discounted at Sigma Sports with over 50% off. Shimano's flagship groupset is designed for the demands of professional racing. It's lighter than Ultegra, but the two share much of the same technology and performance, meaning the decision to go for Dura-Ace often comes down to weight, aesthetics and having the very best. If you've got a frame that deserves a top-tier build, it's an easier justify - especially with 53% off bringing the price down to just £1,699.For most riders, Ultegra is arguably the sweet spot. It delivers almost everything Dura-Ace does, with excellent performance and a well-considered design, but trades a little extra weight for a considerably lower price. At 278g heavier than Dura-Ace, it's a small compromise for the money saved.As an upgrade or a more affordable entry point into electronic shifting, 105 Di2 is a great buy. It retains the 12-speed functionality and semi-wireless set-up of its more expensive siblings, bringing much of the same experience to a lower price point.This is a great opportunity to upgrade to Shimano's 12-speed Di2 electronic shifting for considerably less than usual.

item.title: A pair of race-winning Continental GP5000 S TR tyres plus 500ml of Stan's sealant is now only £99.95 at Merlin Cycles
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: The Continental GP5000 S TR is the tyre of choice for the all-conquering Tadej Pogačar, and is in our opinion, one of the best road bike tyres you can buy, holding the title for best all-round tyre in our best road bike tyres guide and best tubeless tyres guide.Our CN Lab testing also found the GP5000 to be faster than many competitors, including the pro-favourite Vittoria Corsa Pro. That makes them a great choice for performance-focused road bikes, while their impressive lifespan and built-in wear indicators add to their appeal, making it easy to see when it's time for a replacement.Although many pros are adopting even faster TT-specific tyres for road racing, for all-round use (and when you are paying for your tyres), we still think this is the way to go. For UK readers, Merlin Cycles has a very tempting deal on a bundle for just £99.95 down from £182, which includes a pair of the tubeless-ready tyres and 500ml of Stan’s Tubeless Sealant.For US readers, there's no equivalent bundle deal available, but you can still pick up the tyres individually on Amazon, with discounts of up to 18%. The exact saving varies depending on which tyre width you choose.If you haven't yet tried this Tour de France stage-winning rubber, there's never been a better time to pick up a pair, especially with 500ml of tubeless sealant thrown in for under £100.For US readers, there's no bundle deal available, but you can still pick up the Continental GP5000 S TR individually on Amazon, with discounts of up to 18% depending on your chosen tyre width.Continental says the Grand Prix 5000 S TR sets the standard in road tubeless-ready tyre technology.The proof is in the riding, and our own reviewers have put countless miles into testing road tyres across a wide range of conditions. The GP5000 S TR tyres came out on top, earning their place as our benchmark for premium tubeless road performance and scoring a near-perfect 4.5 stars in our in depth review. Our lab testing backed up those real-world findings, confirming Continental's performance claims. Our only real criticisms of the GP5000 S TR tyres are their price and slightly tricky fitting. This deal goes some way to addressing the former, although you'll still need to be prepared for a bit of a battle when mounting them. Having a set of the best tyre levers to hand should make life easier.You can choose between black and tan sidewalls, with black available in widths from 25mm to 35mm and tan from 25mm to 32mm.For the same price as this bundle, Merlin Cycles are currently selling the tyre alone for £49.95, making this bundle particularly good value. If you're considering alternatives, the Michelin Power Cup TLR Folding Road Tyre is our pick for the best budget tyre, which is currently 39% off at Merlin Cycles, bringing it down to £42.95. For something more focused on outright speed, the Vittoria Corsa Pro Speed is also discounted, with 31% off at Winstanleys Bikes, taking it down to £68.49.

item.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Lefty Gomez
item.author: Matt Ferenchick
item.content:encoded: The history of the Yankees’ franchise is generally one defined by hitters. Starting with Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig, the franchise’s most recognizable stars are almost always position players, carrying forward to the modern day with Aaron Judge.However, you cannot win 27 World Series title by throwing out just anyone on the mound. There are still plenty of all-time Yankee greats that were pitchers. One of them was Lefty Gomez, a Hall of Famer in his own right.Vernon Louis “Lefty” Gomez November 26, 1908 (Rodeo, CA) February 17, 1989 (Greenbrae, CA) 1930-42Gomez was one of a number of Yankees of his era to come from California, as he was born there in 1908. His father was of Spanish-Portuguese descent and was a cowboy on a farm north of San Francisco. The kid later known as “Lefty” grew up riding horses and milking cows.In baseball, Gomez grew up playing local sandlot games and was pretty quickly identified as a talent. By 14, he was already getting noticed by the Pacific Coast League’s San Francisco Seals, although they passed on the young, still scrawny Gomez at that time. After his high school career ended, the Seals finally agreed to ink Gomez, although the pitcher had to win over his father, who wished for Lefty to go to college to become an engineer.The Seals farmed out Gomez in 1928, but brought him into the fold for the following season. San Francisco manager Nick Williams was still very skeptical of the still thin and scrawny pitcher, but Gomez eventually broke into the rotation through undeniable performances on the mound. By the end of the season, he was the Seals’ star, leading the league in ERA. The Yankees eventually took notice and signed him in August, but kept him in San Francisco for the rest of the PCL season.Upon reporting to the Yankees for 1930, the team had similar concerns about his frame. They sent Gomez to a “health farm” during spring training. However, he impressed enough to start the year in the big leagues with the team. However, he struggled during his rookie campaign. Not only was he a rookie, but Gomez had suffered an injury after getting hit in the face with a liner back in spring training. Doctors suspected that botched dental work in the aftermath of that had caused an infection that was still bothering the pitcher. Gomez eventually got all his upper teeth pulled and replaced and eventually got sent down to the minor league St. Paul Saints.After a year there, Gomez came back up to the Yankees in 1931, albeit put in the bullpen by new manager Joe McCarthy. However once again, Gomez battled his way into the rotation by simply being too good to deny. By the end of the season, Gomez had won 21 games while posting a 2.67 ERA.Now a full-fledged star of the rotation, Gomez won another 24 games in 1932, although stats like ERA had him a bit below league average for the season. However, his knack for winning got Gomez the start in Game 2 of that year’s Fall Classic, and he delivered. Gomez threw a complete game allowing just two runs, only one of which was earned. The Yankees won the game and the series in a sweep over the Cubs.Over the years, Gomez became a star for the Yankees as they became baseball’s preeminent dynasty. Gomez helped the Yankees to four more World Series titles over the course of his career, as they won a then-record four consecutive titles from 1936-39. Not only did Gomez win five championships in five trips to the Fall Classic, but he put up a perfect 6-0 record as a pitcher. That’s both a World Series and an MLB postseason record for the most wins by a pitcher without having ever taken a loss.Individually, Gomez made seven consecutive All-Star teams from 1933-39. His best year came in 1934, when he won a league-leading 26 games, while also besting baseball in stats like ERA en route to the classic pitching Triple Crown (he won another in 1937), as well as modern ones, including 8.4 rWAR.Gomez also became known as one of the most colorful characters in baseball, getting the nickname “Goofy.” While Yogi Berra has the most notable quotes of anyone in Yankees’ history, Gomez shouldn’t be far behind. Some of his best include replying to a question about whether he would brush back — another thing he was known for — his own mother with a pitch by saying, “You’re damn right I would. She’s a good hitter.”Once while facing Bob Feller, Gomez — a horrifically bad hitter, even for a pitcher — lit a match. When asked by the umpire, “Do you think that match will help you see Feller’s fast one?” Gomez said, “No, I’m not concerned about that. I just want to make sure he can see me.” While filling out a job application following his retirement, Gomez listed the reason for leaving his prior employment as “Couldn’t get anybody out.”In 1939, Gomez suffered an arm injury while covering first base, and that would be the beginning of the end for him. The injury began to affect his pitching motion and he was limited to just 263.2 total innings over the course of the 1940-42 seasons. He did pitch well in the middle of those seasons in 1941, but McCarthy somewhat controversially didn’t use him in the World Series victory over the Dodgers.The injuries eventually caught up to Gomez, and the Yankees released him in January 1943. He signed with the Boston Braves but was released before ever appearing in a game for them. He was picked up by the Washington Senators, and appeared in one game for them, but was released by them too, marking the end of his baseball career.Gomez eventually found his way into coaching and managed in the Yankees’ minor league system, including helming a team with a young Whitey Ford. He later left coaching and had a sales job with Wilson Sporting Goods. Thanks to his affable nature, he also became a popular dinner speaker and talk show guest. Gomez was voted into the Hall of Fame by the Veterans Committee in 1972. He eventually settled back in his native California, where he resided until passing away in 1989 at age 80.Lefty Gomez was an undeniably great pitcher. However, it’s debatable whether he would’ve been as well remembered had he not been a member of those great Yankees teams and was putting up those stats for a middling one. However, he was a reason those Yankees’ teams were as good as they were. After all, you can’t win championships with outstanding talent on just one side of the ball.See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

item.title: 'The only way for the race to grow' – Women’s Festival Elsy Jacobs race becomes part of themen'sTour of Luxembourg organisation
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Organisers of the Tour de Luxembourg men’s race will take over organisation of the women’s Festival Elsy Jacobs from 2027, has learnt.The race, named after the first-ever women’s World Champion, began in 2008 and has taken various formats over the years, even expanding to a three-day stage race. Under the new management, it will return as a two-stage race, moving from its traditional spot in the spring to take its place on the morning of the weekend stages of the men’s Tour de Luxembourg, scheduled for September 18 and 19, 2027.The event will remain as a 2.1, third-tier event for the time being, though the new organisation has hopes of it moving up to the Women’s ProTour level at the earliest opportunity in 2029, joining the men’s event as a second-division race.Since its inception in 2008, Festival Elsy Jacobs has been run by SAF Zeisseng, a local cycling club from the Luxembourg City suburb of Cessanges. However, since the 2020 race was cancelled due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the race has struggled, dropping the prologue in 2023 before becoming two standalone 1.1 races the following year."The change is the only way for the race to grow and not to disappear," organiser Michel Zangerlé told . "The association of the Tour de Luxembourg for men will take over, with us in support. That means we are not out, but the other organisation is the leader for every financial topic."Despite the new structure, the race will retain its name, its heritage being important to the new organisation."It’s not Skoda Tour de Luxembourg Femmes or something like that; it will keep the identity of Elsy Jacobs," General Secretary of the Tour de Luxembourg, Benoît Theisen, told . "We want to give the know-how we have in the men’s race and the setup of the men's race exactly the same as for the women. And for us, it was the only way to do it was to combine it in one date because if you have it on a second date, you need the full infrastructure again."It’s something new; we are really excited. It will be a new start, but we don't start from zero because there's this big heritage."The original race would always have at least one day in Jacobs’ birthplace of Garnich, and while the 2027 race start and finish locations of the stages are not yet public, it’s highly unlikely this will continue, though clearly the race’s survival is far more important.One of the issues the original organisation faced was the haphazard way in which the women’s calendar has expanded as the sport became more professional. Its regular place at the end of April meant that, since 2023, it clashed with the Vuelta España Femenina. That meant the race was no longer able to attract the biggest teams and riders, affecting sponsorship.While it was never a big name on the calendar, the original organisation was always a trailblazer, introducing a live stream of the action as far back as 2017, when the majority of World Tour races were not shown live.It has also been won by some of the biggest names in the sport, with Marianne Vos, Emma Pooley, Anna van der Breggen and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney all featuring on its palmarès.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: If you're looking for the best urban e-bike helmet, we've found it, and it's got a $39 saving in this Black Friday cycling deal
item.author: Rich Owen
item.content:encoded: If you're an urban e-bike rider or cycle commuter looking for extra helmet protection, the Smith Dispatch MIPS is an excellent choice. We rate it as our best e-bike helmet overall because it looks great, is comfortable to wear, and comes with an array of built-in safety features.The only downside is its top-end MRSP, but right now you can save $39 on the usual price in this Black Friday cycling deal.The Dispatch is one of the most well-put-together e-bike helmets you can buy. As well as its sleek looks, it's lightweight for its class (13.9oz for size L) and has NTA 8776 certification – a tougher safety standard specifically for e-bike helmets. It also comes with a rechargeable, integrated rear light.While it is at the top end of the e-bike price bracket, we reckon overall performance justifies its price tag – and it's currently available for far less than usual in this Black Friday deal.394g / 13.9oz (size L)YesMatte black, matte whiteIf you're riding an e-bike, going beyond the protection of a regular helmet is a good idea due to the additional forces at play from higher riding speeds and greater momentum. The Dispatch comes with the e-bike-specific NTA 8776 certificate, which means it's been tested at higher-speed impacts and provides additional head coverage compared to standard helmets. It also combines MIPS (a system which protects the head from rotational forces during a crash) with Koroyd crumple zones strategically placed within the helmet.Our cycle commuting expert rated the Dispatch's AirEvac visor venting as one of the helmet's standout extra features. The vents direct incoming air downwards to stop your glasses from steaming up. The other eight vents are smaller, but cope well even on purely pedal-powered commutes, plus their smaller size means less water getting in when it rains.The rear safety light is another neat extra. It's rechargeable, removable, and has three light modes – constant, rapid flash or a slow flash.

item.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous

item.title: Visma steps down as title sponsor of Visma-Lease a Bike team
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: Visma-Lease a Bike have confirmed that Visma will no longer be part of the team name in 2027, with the Norwegian software company stepping down from its title sponsorship role but not leaving the team completely. Such a move has been on the cards for months, and it was first reported back in February that Visma was looking to reduce the level of its investment, but the exact nature of the relationship from 2027 was made official on Thursday. The team announced that Visma will become a 'Founding Partner' of both men's and women's teams, in a similar move to another former title sponsor, Jumbo. "As part of this new partnership structure, Visma will no longer serve as the team’s name partner," read a statement from the team."The designation of Founding Partner recognises the role Visma has played in the team’s development since 2019, a period marked by continuous innovation and fantastic sporting success."It is not yet clear who will step in as a co-title sponsor in 2027, with team management conducting an extensive sponsorship search for much of this year. As it stands, the team has simply been registered by the name of its holding company, Yellow B, in the initial application process for 2027 UCI WorldTour and Women's WorldTour licences.Visma began its sponsorship of the team in 2019, and its title sponsorship coincided with a hugely successful period in which the team won 10 men's Grand Tours, including all three in the same season in 2023, and the 2025 Tour de France Femmes.“It’s fantastic that Visma is extending its partnership with our team. Visma believed in our ambitions when we started working together in 2019," said team boss Richard Plugge."Since then, we’ve shared moments we could only dream of back then. I’m grateful to everyone at Visma for the trust they’ve placed in us over the years. Having Visma stay with the team as a Founding Partner reflects what we’ve built together."Visma's CEO Merete Hverven was also quoted in the announcement, explaining that the company's "strategic priorities have evolved" as it has expanded from the Nordic region into Europe and Latin America. Rather than the title nature of the sponsorship being brought to an end, this was framed within the context of several of Visma's subsidiary brands coming on board as minor sponsors from 2027. "This strategic evolution is reflected in the updated partnership, where several of Visma’s leading national brands across Europe, offering accounting software for SMBs, will have their logos showcased on the team jersey next season. Those sponsors will be revealed at a later date.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
