item.title: Knicks 121, Cavaliers 102: “The most Mike Brown victory imaginable”
item.author: Moritz Wollert
item.content:encoded: It’s easy to get lost in today’s world. Everything is spinning so fast, so many things are out of control. Prices, taxes, wars, narratives, diabolical devices, our sense of togetherness. Life sometimes feels like an endless list of things that, no matter how much you scratch off, no matter what you decide not to worry about, gets longer by the minute. The NBA is no exception, a cutthroat world infected by influencing influences that expects daily reinvention, that wants to turn humans into brands and expand like a kraken gobbling up the last little dollars from the deepest pits of the coral reef.As you watch another foul-baiting baller be rewarded for his deeds, followed by the 23rd commercial for guaranteed grifting, it can be tough to find the joy here from time to time, to remember why you ever thought this was fun. But then Jose Alvarado runs into the picture and steals a ball, only to rise up moments later for a three. He jumps for joy as he hits it, just like the little kid he once was on the playgrounds of the city that he now represents on the biggest stage there is in basketball. And you smile along with him.Jose Alvarado carries the Knicks to victoryThere is something inherently right about a guy like Jose Alvarado. Sure, he is an annoying pest defensively, loudmouthed, confident on his good days, cocky on his better ones. A guy you would probably hate if he wasn’t on your team. Not even in the fun way of hating an opponent, if there is one. No, you really can’t stand that little bugger, like, at all. Yet even if you root for some other franchise whose name doesn’t rhyme with clicks, deep down inside your basketball fan’s heart, you have to appreciate a guy, a man, a kid like Jose Alvarado. Mike Brown surely does.It didn’t even take Alvarado’s tide-turning performance in the Knicks’ 121-102 destruction of the Cleveland Cavaliers in yesterday’s NBA Cup game, which was, as PolyphonicSpreewell so beautifully put it in the , “the most Mike Brown victory imaginable.” It didn’t take his 16 points in the fourth quarter or his 21 in total. But the light shining on Jose surely was a reminder that the big little Puerto Rican embodies what this New York basketball team is. Sure, they can beat you with Xs and Os, with the might of majestic superstars, with firepower that can put a New Year’s fireworks display to shame. But there is more that makes the Knicks the Knicks. A group that has a heart and a soul beyond what is expected of them, some inner power they can turn to when things go sideways. Something that lets them play and, more importantly, enjoy the game innocently, freely. How it was supposed to be experienced.Alvarado is not your type of guy? , says Pacôme Djenon Dadiet! It didn’t matter that he didn’t really hit shots consistently yesterday or, frankly, ever before. He still plunged into the action versus the James Hardens and Donovan Mitchells of the world like the Knicks’ bench was a cliff and his name was Orlando Duque. Maybe not as gracefully, but definitely just as committed and energetic. And, most importantly, without any fear. There was no fear in Tyler Nickel, either, who at some point seemed as far away from real NBA minutes as his birthplace in the Shenandoah Valley is from Madison Square Garden. But don’t worry, bench guy, Mike Brown’s got a map, and he knows where to find you.Mike Brown works his magic with the KnicksWith injuries to OG Anunoby, Deuce McBride, and Jordan Clarkson, plus ineffective and almost shockingly bad nights from Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns, the coach seemingly didn’t have to search yesterday. He just hurled everyone he had on his pine into the action and watched them stick it to the Cavs. Mo Diawara hit a three. James Wiseman dominated the paint for stretches in the fourth quarter. He didn’t look out of place; he didn’t look like he didn’t know what he was doing. Rather, he played like a man possessed, not by some evil power or the One Ring to rule them all, but by the unwavering confidence and belief of a bald, happy-go-lucky man who coaches champions.These champions include a much-maligned Mikal Bridges, who carried the team throughout the entire second quarter. They also include Josh Hart and Landry Shamet, who did their thing and then some. They are all guys who had rough goes in the past but who never found themselves in Mr. Brown’s doghouse. They deserve to be singled out for pushing the ball in transition, for point-of-attack defense, for just being themselves. But frankly, who doesn’t? Everyone did a little and then a lot of what was needed from them. I’m sure Tyler Kolek was one of the biggest cheerleaders despite his rough night on the court. It all speaks to the culture that Mike Brown has bestowed upon this team, that he has created with all of his players. All of them. All these guys who know what hard work is. Who relish every opportunity they get.And who have a way of playing basketball that is as much fun as you can imagine.

item.title: It’s never been cheaper for Chris Froome to give you directions with this big brand busting bike computer deal for Black Friday
item.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
item.content:encoded: I reviewed the iGPSPORT BiNavi bike computer earlier this year and was both surprised and impressed. Now this Chinese bike computer is on sale for Black Friday, and it offers performance that's on a par with far more expensive touch screen units. For me, it's an absolute bargain and our best budget bike computer right now. Black Friday kicks off tomorrow, and the tech team is hunting for the best deals across all the sales. If you are shopping for a bike computer, consider the BiNavi, created by iGPSPORT, sponsor of Groupama-FDJ United. This unit is easy to use, fast and powerful, with good mapping. I tested it for close to 1,000 miles this summer and was generally impressed with its performance. The BiNavi has 15% off in the US; this is a heck of a lot of computer for just over $200. The iGPSPORT app also works well and allows you to customise and update the computer unit. This is a great price for a computer that performs as well as units that cost a lot more money. Big colour screen, fast - what's not to like? Check out our review for a lot more information. The BiNavi is a touschcreen bike computer with a competitive spec list: 102g / 3.6oz 3.5” 32 GB Connectivity: ANT+ / Bluetooth / WIFI IPX7 35+ hours, depending on use.It's fast, and the user interface is easy to use and navigate. It's compatibe with platforms like Strava and Trining Peaks which made it seamless when uploading my sessions. Support from the app is good, and it allows for things like on device music control, heck, you can even have cycling legend Chris Froome narrate your GPS instructions. I had a couple of glitches, and feel the screen isn't as vivid as more premium units, though in use it wasn't an issue. Certain navigation functions also weren't as seamless as say the Hammerhead Karoo. If you wan't a computer for all your training and riding, and don't rely on mapping every ride. The BiNavi offers a solid platform and excellent value.

item.title: Lapierre on the brink of salvation with court studying multiple offers, as a former pro cyclist 'really wants to acquire' the French bike brand
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Lapierre is among the brands which Dublin-based Quanta Capital is hoping to save after the collapse of the Accell Group, can confirm.Last week the Sunday Times reported that a deal to acquire the French bike manufacturer, along with historic British bike brand Raleigh, had been done, but the transaction is not yet complete, according to Lapierre's Directeur Général William Perrier.Lapierre, which supplies bikes to the Picnic-PostNL team, was founded in 1946 and has been making bikes in the French city of Dijon ever since. It was bought by Accell Group in 1996, but since the parent company’s collapse in August of this year, it has been in court supervised administration, allowing a six-month observation period from September 21 to find new investment."We had some offers on the table, and more recently, beginning of this week, we were in front of the court to do a check after the offers and to have a clear status [on] where we are and what we still have to work on to make it happen," Perrier told . "I will only comment the Lapierre part, but of course Quanta is one of the candidates, but from now on the court did not take any decision."We are looking at it, but I don't want to promise too much, right? We are still working on having a new owner, nothing is 100% signed."Accell, which owned a number of other cycling brands, struggled after the Covid-19 pandemic. In late July it was due to be bought by the Singapore-based DuTech Holdings, but Accell was declared bankrupt five days later, and the deal fell through, leaving its brands high and dry, though DuTech has since acquired some of Accell’s other brands.Led by former pro cyclist Mel Sutcliffe, Quanta Capital’s interest in some of Accell’s brands was rumoured and confirmed soon after the collapse, and now it seems close to fruition."So there is still some discussion between all the parties to check the financing part, the social part, the overall project in order to sign the deal. But as of today, of course, Quanta is one of the potential bidders who really wants to acquire Lapierre," Perrier continued."But this morning [Thursday, November 26] I can tell you that it is not yet the case. There is like a lot of discussion ongoing. We are still working normally, we are still producing bikes in Dijon. We are still delivering as much as possible [to] our dealers and our final customers."Sutcliffe declined to comment when approached by and a request for comment has since gone unanswered.British bike brand Raleigh was acquired by Accell in 2012, but although Quanta is confirmed as being interested in the brand, with the Sunday Times reporting the deal is done, there seems little left to save. In late September the Nottingham Post reported that a total of 43 employees had been made redundant, with only two retained, and that the company’s remaining stock had been sold to UK Bike retail chain Halfords for more than £7m.The administrators’ report stated: "No part of the trading business was transferred as a going concern as this was ceased immediately upon our appointment." That leaves the Raleigh trademark, which is still owned by Accell and its creditors.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. Plus, the Cyclingnews app means you can stay up-to-date wherever you go!

item.title: Castelli's warmest winter cycling jacket is on sale, with one variant offering a mind blowing £272 saving in early Black Friday sale
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: The Alpha 150 is the Italian brand’s most wintery and most expensive outer layer best suited to long, steady rides at temperatures of around 7 and 12ºC (44-54 ºF).At full price, it's a lot of money to spend on a jacket, but the Castelli Alpha 150 jacket is now available for less in both the UK and US with these Black Friday deals. For UK readers, the men's Alpha 150 is 25% off in black, with most sizes currently available. The women's version has an even bigger discount, with 76% off the Hibiscus colourway in size XS, while the black version is 30% off across all sizes. In the US, the men's jacket is 40% off in black, dropping from $420 to $252, with other colourways discounted by 25%.Our Senior Tech Writer, Will Jones, describes it as a warm, comfortable and highly breathable jacket, making it a great choice for cold-weather riding, although those regularly riding in freezing temperatures may want something more heavily insulated.Castelli’s jacket range has gone on a fair old journey in recent years. The Gabba and Perfetto have been overhauled, and everything is now PFAS-free.The main fabric of the Alpha 150 is Castelli’s exclusive ‘150g Polartec® AirCore™ electrospun air-permeable membrane’, which is alleged to be windproof while also remaining highly breathable. If it's going to rain, you'll want to wear something else though. Open up the main double zip and you’ll reveal a Polartec Alpha inbuilt gilet which is very well executed. The rear panel is free-floating, attached only at the sides and top so it articulates more easily. The form is tailored but not skin-tight, with enough room to layer up a little bit underneath, at least with a thicker long-sleeve jersey and a winter base layer. Overall, this is a very good jacket that Will enjoyed wearing, offering a comfortable fit and excellent breathability. However, while it's a great option for cold-weather riding, its suggested temperature range may be a little optimistic. Will found that it wasn't particularly suited to temperatures below around 5°C, especially if you plan on stopping for any length of time.If you're considering alternatives to the Alpha 150, other winter jackets currently discounted include:

item.title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
item.author: Scott K. Johnson
item.content:encoded: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

item.title: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
item.author: Ars Staff
item.content:encoded:
Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We've got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist "here's my laptop and monitor" setups to "I really like collecting things." Without any further ado, let's dig in: Living in a New York apartment means being smart with available space. Credit: Jeremy Hsu/Ars Technica
As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.

item.title: The Magicshine SEEMEE 300 rear light boasts a huge 300 lumens and 200-hour battery life, and it's now 40% off for Black Friday
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: The Magicshine SEEMEE 300 is one of the best rear bike lights we've tested, combining a wealth of features with market-leading battery life and a very reasonable price tag. However, the SEEMEE 300 still has plenty going for it, with three key advantages over its newer sibling - longer battery life, additional side visibility thanks to its downward-facing LED, and, of course, a lower price. Our Senior Tech Writer, Will Jones, found very little to fault with the SEEMEE 300, awarding it a near-perfect 96% score following his testing. Will only marked it down for the slightly confusing mode selections. With 40% off for Black Friday dropping it to just £35.99 ($41.79 in the USA), it's an even more tempting buy.It may have been superseded by its 400 sibling as our best rear bike light but this older model still does some things other lights on the market don’t in terms of battery life and additional visibility. The SEEMEE 300 boasts one of the longest battery lives of any rear light on the market, offering up to 200 hours in Eco mode and comfortably outlasting its newer sibling, the SEEMEE 400, which tops out at 107 hours because of the higher overall power output of the 400 lumens. It also offers great side visibility with the downward-facing LED on the underside that projects a red cone around you to make sure you're seen from all angles.Smart features are now pretty frequently seen on the best rear bike lights and the SEEMEE 300 is no exception. These include an auto-dim function, which adjusts the light's output to suit ambient lighting conditions, helping to preserve its already impressive battery life. There's also a motion sensor that acts as a brake light, increasing the light's output when you slow down which is a particularly useful addition if you're riding in traffic.Other rear lights currently discounted include:

item.title: The most dramatic moments of the 2026 cycling season – Shock retirements, nail-biting sprints and tense transfers
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: 2026 is coming to an end, with training camps about to begin and attention already shifting to the 2027 racing season. Here at , we've already been reviewing many aspects of the season just gone, such as the best neo pros and best domestiques, but what about the moments that defined the year?Rather than best moments – because who could ever choose just 10? – we've gone back through the headlines to identify the 10 most dramatic moments of the 2026 season, the stories that shocked all of us and the racing that got the excitement brewing. From sudden retirements and high-profile crashes to tensions bubbling over at the biggest races on the calendar, as well as thrilling sprints and a debate about anti-doping, here are the 10 moments that we think delivered the drama in 2026.Simon Yates' shock retirementRewind all the way to the start of the year, and things kicked off with a bang before the racing had even really started, with Simon Yates shocking the world with the news of his retirement. Rumours of Yates thinking about an early exit from the sport had been swirling, but after he'd won the Giro d'Italia, completed the 2025 season and started winter training and 2026 camps with Visma-Lease a Bike, it seemed like that must be off the table. Apparently not.One day he was out training in Visma kit, and the next he announced his retirement just a few days into January. It was a surprise to not just the cycling world, but to his team too, who were then left scrambling and a rider short for the rest of the season. To bow out on such a high, as the Giro champion with a full and busy schedule, is practically unheard of and dominated the headlines for weeks as we collected reactions from around the peloton – mainly equally as surprised as we were. Even to this day, Yates has not opened up all that much about why he made his decision when he did, instead just slipping back into normal life. Whilst it might not have felt that dramatic to him, it was certainly one of the defining moments of the first part of the 2026 season. A frightening crash at Milan-San Remo WomenI wouldn't usually include a crash in a list like this, but if I am thinking of moments that were shocking and dramatic to their core, the scary crash involving Debora Silvestri, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Kim Le Court-Pienaar at Milan-San Remo Women was one of them. Coming off the Cipressa at high speed, several riders came down hard, with Silvestri the worst off as she crashed over the guardrails and fell several feet onto concrete.This isn't the kind of drama we want to celebrate or remember, but it was a frightening moment that raised questions about safety, speed and risk – questions that would continue through the season. Silvestri's myriad of injuries and long stay in hospital, including needing breathing support, was a stark reminder of just how much danger cyclists face with very, very little protection between them and hitting the tarmac and over 60kph. The intense debate about safety hadn't quite kicked off back in March, but it became a defining conversation of the 2026 season, and this crash will go down as one of the types of incidents we must work harder to avoid, or at least offer riders more protection from.The final sprint of men's Paris-RoubaixThe final sprint of Paris-Roubaix is always one of cycling's most electrifying moments, and this year was no different, with the velodrome finales of both the men's and women's races offering spectacular, hold-your-breath racing. Franziska Koch bettering both Marianne Vos and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot was an enormous underdog win moment in the women's race, but the one that will really, really stick with me is the climax of the men's race. The whole race was packed to the brim with drama, to be truthful, but that was distilled into a few minutes of pure adrenaline as the leaders entered the Roubaix velodrome. Wout van Aert vs Tadej Pogačar. Knowing what we do about both riders it felt in a way like the story might already be written. Van Aert is the rider more likely to win Roubaix, given the reigning Tour de France champion is usually nowhere near the top of the list of favourites. But the mythology of these two riders made it different; Pogačar is the rider who wins at will, and Van Aert is the one who has been runner-up more times than you can count. I had a sinking feeling that the Belgian star was going to be denied yet again by the specialism-defying Slovenian.That's why, when Van Aert drew slightly ahead of Pogačar in the sprint and soared to a fantastic win, it felt like a shock and a huge moment. It was somehow the obvious result and one that felt like it could easily slip through Van Aert's fingers, but it didn't. Pogačar had been beaten – a very rare occurrence indeed – and Van Aert had scored his first cobbled Monument win in a wildly emotional moment. It was a gripping sprint to round out a hugely dramatic race, and is surely one of the most memorable moments of 2026.Falling ice on the Colle delle FinestreThe penultimate stage of the women's Giro d'Italia should have been one of the most dramatic days of the women's calendar as they went up and over the Colle delle Finestre, but it ended up delivering the drama in different ways than we expected.Instead of going up and over the mythical gravel climb and climbing back up to Sestriere for the finish, the stage was shortened mid-race due to the risk of falling ice of the top of the Finestre. This meant that the Giro's most epic stage was suddenly turned on its head, with riders having to adapt their tactics and plans on the road, leading to an all-out battle on the climb – which, ironically, might not have happened had the stage maintained its full length.Four riders came towards the revised finish line together, with Demi Vollering powering away from Bella Holmgren, Antonia Niedermaier and Anna van der Breggen to pull closer to the overall lead, which she would go on to grab away from Van der Breggen on the final stage. All this unfolded in the ominous mist atop the Finestre, making for truly dramatic scenes.Overnight testing debate at the Tour de France The Tour de France hasn't faced actual doping drama for several years now, with a few unfruitful raids the most we've seen and a long way away from the mid-race positives and expulsions we were used to seeing a few years ago. But the 2026 edition still found a way to weave a controversial doping storyline into its plot.The drama ended up not being about doping itself, but testing, when several top names including Pogačar and Vingegaard revealed that they had been woken in the middle of the night by testers. Gloss over the fact that riders aren't actually meant to reveal stuff like that – the anti-doping authority's element of surprise is a bit undermined if riders understand their tactics – and it was soon pretty much the biggest story of the middle of the race. Debate raged on over whether it was ethical to wake tired riders in the early hours as they tried to recover before another stage, and about whether this meant there was suspicion over the riders involved (to be clear, such tests do not imply any suspicion).As far as we're aware, nothing came of those midnight tests, with the date for results to be returned long gone by now, but it certainly brought the topic of testing and doping back into the spotlight at the Tour, and stirred up the drama in a race that wasn't exactly full of that racing-wise.Jonas Vingegaard crashes out of the TourThe first of two really dramatic GC crashes over the summer, Jonas Vingegaard's Tour de France was over in the blink of an eye when he crashed heavily on a nondescript corner on stage 15. It was clear pretty quickly that he was not going to continue, as he clutched his arm in a way we all recognise as a surefire sign of a broken collarbone – an injury no one can race through. It was a shocking and sad sight, and heavily shaped the rest of the race. Suddenly, the only rider who has ever challenged Tadej Pogačar at the Tour was out of the running, and even if he was already 4:30 down at that stage, any tiny hope of a miraculous turnaround was definitively gone. It felt like Pogačar's fifth win was confirmed in that moment. As it turned out, that one crash would go on to have further reaching effects than we could have imagined at the time, with Vingegaard ultimately opting not to return to racing at all in 2026, and rumours even brewing that retirement was on his mind after another big crash in the sport he has already criticised for being too dangerous. Thankfully, he's since confirmed that he's not bowing out just yet, but that crash may still go down as a defining moment in his career. A wild weekend in Nice to close out the Tour de France FemmesIf fans had felt that the Tour de France hadn't been dramatic enough in terms of the racing and results, the Tour de France Femmes came along and said 'hold my beer'. The start of the race was a bit of a slowburn, admittedly, but as we arrived in Nice for the final weekend, the temperature – both literal and metaphorical – was turned up to the max. First was the bitter clash between Célia Gery and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, with the Polish rider angrily confronting Gery and accusing her of deliberately blocking her in order to benefit Demi Vollering, with something of a war of words ensuing over the next 24 hours. On top of that, Marlen Reusser suffered a nasty crash on the final stage that saw her tumble off the podium – after previously being in the lead and fighting for the win – and roll into Nice heartbroken and in tears. And that's all without mentioning the race itself, which saw three different riders wear yellow over the final four days, with a battle for seconds right up until the final finish line in one of the most thrilling editions of the women's Tour we've seen yet. It was tense and sweltering under the Nice sun, and feelings definitely boiled over at times, which is why this goes down as one of the most dramatic weekends of the season. Tadej Pogačar crashes out of the VueltaThe second major GC crash-out of the season was even more dramatic that Vingegaard's. Pogačar is a rider who crashes relatively rarely, so to see him go head-over-handlebars, whilst in the red jersey and the overwhelming favourite to win the Vuelta a España, was shocking and almost unbelievable, so rare is such an incident. We think a small rock in the road was to blame for one of the worst crashes of Pogačar's career, and not just because it dramatically took away his chance of completing his Grand Tour set, but because he suffered some truly nasty injuries. He suffered a concussion, a fractured collarbone, and three fractured vertebrae, having to undergo surgery and a significant stay in hospital. The crash changed the course of the Vuelta – Enric Mas soared to victory in the race that looked nailed-on for Pogačar – but also the whole rest of the season, with new faces coming to the fore at the World Championships, Euros and Il Lombardia, races which the Slovenian has previously dominated. In many ways, Pogačar's crash was the defining moment of the latter part of 2026, and a healthy dose of drama for the rider who often seems to glide right past any misfortune. Riders protest the start of Il LombardiaI'll admit, I don't usually tune in for the flag to flag coverage of Il Lombardia, because what's actually going to happen in the first hour of such a long race? But it became clear pretty quickly that anyone not watching the start of this year's race had missed a surreal moment, as the riders staged a protest about rider safety. In many ways, what stands out about this moment is that, whilst impactful, it in itself actually that dramatic. There was no song and dance or outburst of frustration, just a quiet standstill in solidarity with the increasing dangers the peloton seems to be facing, and an emotive but firm speech from Remco Evenepoel.But it was dramatic in the sense of being surprising and headline-making, and it was all anyone talked about for most of the day, until Paul Seixas took over the narrative with his emphatic win. It felt like – probably belatedly – something of a watershed moment, riders making it clear as a whole that the incidents that have affected the peloton this year are simply not acceptable, and setting out the possibility that riders may just refuse to race if changes are not made. It's been an issue that was brewing all season, and really came to a head in the final weeks of the year. Hopefully, that can manifest in real improvements in 2027 and beyond.Paula Blasi exits UAE Team L'ImadOur final dramatic moment was less of a single moment, but a dramatic saga that dragged out over the whole season, with various moments of tension before the situation was finally resolved in October. Paula Blasi should have had the best year of her career so far, winning La Vuelta Femenina and Amstel Gold Race in only her first full year as a WorldTour rider, but instead she became embroiled in a difficult and often very public transfer drama. The Spaniard decided early in the year that UAE Team L'Imad was no longer the right environment for her, and though a relatively straightforward three-party agreement and pay-out would allow her to move to a new team – as multiple riders have done in the last few years – but what ensued instead was a fairly unpleasant struggle, with UAE attempting to block the move, talking Blasi down in the press, and supposed rider tensions becoming a particular sore spot at the Tour de France Femmes. This was all paired with trouble behind the scenes at UAE, who let go of their team principal prematurely and have struggled to find a full time replacement.In the end, Blasi's move to Movistar did finally go through after a great deal of negotiating, and the 23-year-old seems to be much happier after reporting some really difficult times that even made her question whether she belonged in cycling. A year that should have been remembered for her breakthrough successes may well be remembered for this conflict instead, so she and her new team will be hoping it's only her results that make the headlines in 2027.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: 'Ridiculous and stupid' – Mads Pedersen hits out at UCI contract rules which sees riders wearing old teams' kit to new team training camps
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Mads Pedersen has hit out at the UCI contract rule requiring riders to wear their old kit at their new team's training camps.This week, Primož Roglič and Richard Carapaz have been seen wearing Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe and EF Education-EasyPost kits as they met up with NSN for the first time, and in the coming weeks we'll see more and more of these out-of-place kits during teams' December camps.It's all down to UCI regulations, which mean contracts run to December 31, meaning riders are still representing their 'old' teams until the New Year. Regulation 2.15.139 reads, 'The riders may not, for the duration of the present contract, work for any other team or advertise for any other sponsors…'Speaking on his podcast, Pedersen called the regulation "ridiculous and stupid.""You could simply include a clause stating that in the event of a team switch from December 1 – or from the first training camp – you are allowed to use your new team’s equipment," he said."That would make it so easy. Then you wouldn’t have all that nonsense anymore, and you would prevent riders from missing out on their pay in December because they were riding a Ridley while contractually they were required to ride a Trek."Pedersen will witness a host of riders in their old team's kit when his Lidl-Trek team meet up in Spain next month. Key new signings Filippo Ganna, Felix Gall, and Jordan Jegat will be wearing Netcompany Ineos, Decathlon CMA CGM, and TotalEnergies kits."We are working on it with the AIGCP [the association of professional cycling teams] and the CPA riders' union," he said."The regulation change will definitely happen, with contracts starting on November 1. The starting year is yet to be determined in consultation with all stakeholders."Riders and teams favour changing the rules, and the UCI was reportedly seeking to do so, yet the rules remain in place, drawing complaints from fans and the peloton.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Primož Roglič tempted by each Grand Tour in 2027, but a decision is several weeks away
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: Primož Roglič has not yet made a decision on his race calendar for 2027, saying it was “way too early” given he only signed for his new team, NSN Cycling, little over a week ago. But he did say that all three of the Grand Tours are tempting him in their own way. Roglič has won the Vuelta a España a joint-record four times, and he also has a Giro d’Italia title to his name from 2023, with the Tour de France the one missing from his palmarès. Next year, the Giro d’Italia represents something of a draw, given the race heads into his native Slovenia, first on stage 1, then an entirely Slovenian stage the next day. The Tour de France, meanwhile, might represent some of that “unfinished business” he spoke about this week, especially after not racing it this year. And the Vuelta of course is the Grand Tour where he has made his name and stands a chance of becoming the outright record holder with five titles, after showcasing his persisting Grand Tour credentials with the runner-up spot this year. "Actually, we sat down together with the directors and a couple of guys, and then we started talking, you know," Roglič said during a first round of interviews from the NSN Cycling training camp in Spain this week. "The Giro starts almost in Slovenia, the second stage is in Slovenia, the Zoncolan [on stage 20] is not far from Slovenia… nice. "The Tour de France, I was not there last year. It’s missing me… nice. "The Vuelta, you know… also nice."Roglič has clearly started mulling things over but insisted no decision has been taken yet, saying he has other business to attend to first, namely meeting all his new teammates and staff, as well as familiarising himself with his new equipment. "Later on, hopefully, yes, we start to make more seriously a deeper program, and from that, we can also define which Grand Tours I would like to do."We can also then make a [plan for the] start of the season, but for sure I will not start early in Australia or something like that."NSN Cycling’s general manager Kjell Carlstrom also insisted it was too early to decide where Roglič will race in 2027, indicating that they will wait for the route for the Vuelta a España to be revealed on January 14. "The other thing that we definitely want to see is the the Vuelta route and how that is designed because we believe that without knowing what the Grand Tours look like, it's impossible to build a complete calendar," Carlstrom told ."Then you have to start from the Grand Tours and which ones it would be. Because I would presume that he has the capacity to do more than one, and on a good level. So we need to look at this carefully before we decide where he's going."We only spoke really with him yesterday in terms of getting to understand him better, what type of rider he really is, from the character perspective, and what he likes, what he doesn't like, and all these things, which are very important when you plan a calendar. "Now the performance team needs to really take this into consideration and try to set down a draft plan of what it could look like."While it’s too early to say where Roglič will race, the team have already confirmed a partial plan for their other star signing, Richard Carapaz, who is heading to the Giro d’Italia in May. Carapaz will certainly race two Grand Tours in 2027 but at this point it has not been confirmed whether that will be the Tour or Vuelta, with that decision again likely to be made after the Vuelta route reveal, and in collaboration with Roglič's schedule. Carapaz has confirmed his intention to target the GC at the Giro, with Carlstrom indicating he could opt for "differing goals" – ie stage wins – in his second Grand Tour of the year. Carlstrom insisted the two riders could dovetail well, but Roglič spoke of “sharing the calendar” with his new teammate. That, and given another new climber signing, Santiago Buitrago, is also set for the Giro, would make it unlikely that Roglič heads to Italy in May, even with the draw of the Slovenian stages. The Tour de France and Vuelta a España, then, would appear to be the logical combination. The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
item.author: Frédéric Noy
item.content:encoded: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technicalIn the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric NoyContinue reading...

item.title: Knicks 121, Cavs 102: Scenes from a second-half bench bash
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: The Knicks’ hopes of repeating as NBA Cup champions hinged on beating Cleveland (9-10) tonight and Miami on Friday, while Philadelphia had to beat Miami (which they did) and Indiana has to topple Philadelphia. Even then, advancement would come down to point differential, meaning New York (12-6) would likely need to win both games by double digits.Consider the mission half completed. As you could deduce from the blazing blue court at Madison Square Garden, tonight’s tilt was a Cup game. Three Knicks were sidelined by injury: OG Anunoby, Miles McBride, and Jordan Clarkson. Anunoby’s absence was felt as the Cavaliers scored 61 first-half points (and a lopsided free-throw disparity stung, too). The adjustments Mike Brown made in the locker room paid dividends on the court. His squad applied stingier defense, got their turnovers under control, won the fourth quarter 39-17, and flipped the game to win, 121-102.Of the six Knicks with double-digit points tonight, Jose Alvarado’s barrage of fourth-quarter triples and his season-high / team-high 21 were arguably the most impactful. On a short-handed night, and with multiple starters playing through injury, Jose was once again prepared to step into the spotlight and contribute meaningful minutes. What a professional! What depth!Three consecutive turnovers didn’t help (two by Karl-Anthony Towns, one by Josh Hart) as the Knicks fell behind early in the first quarter. Midway through the period, Jalen Brunson scored seven in under two minutes to regain the lead. In this streaky contest, though, it made sense that he missed his next five attempts. Towns (12 PTS, 10 RBS, 7 AST, +21) was a game-time decision due to knee soreness, and his scoring showed the limp, producing a single point in the frame. Filling in for Anunoby in the first five, Landry Shamet made his sixth start of the season. He finished with a tidy 11 points on three made three-pointers.The quarter was competitive until the final three minutes. After Pacôme Dadiet (yes, him!) drilled a triple to pull the Knicks within one, Cleveland rattled off a 10-0 run, powered by five consecutive points from Meleek Thomas, two Thomas Bryant free throws, and a Donovan Mitchell and-one. The latter easily had the biggest impact on the quarter, tallying 14 points, three dimes, and a steal. As for New York’s bench support, Dadiet (7 PTS, 14 MIN) provided positive defensive efforts with a block and a steal, but neither Tyler Kolek nor Andre Drummond moved the needle. New York managed just six points over the final five-ish minutes, and Cleveland closed the quarter ahead, 34-23.To start the second, the good guys outscored the villains by ten, chiseling an 11-point deficit to one. Credit Towns and his four points, two dimes, and two blocks for the comeback. Mohamed Diawara lent a triple, too, and Mikal Bridges found his rhythm, blasting out seven fast points. Naturally, Cleveland responded with a 9-2 stretch when James Harden (28 PTS, 1-8 3PT) finally got on the board. Dadiet drizzled water on our good feelings by missing three straight shots, and Brunson still couldn’t regain his touch, going scoreless from the field in the period.Playing from 55-44 down with four minutes left in the half, the hosts posted 11 unanswered points, eight of which belonged to Bridges. He’d finish the half with 17 points. This, my friends, is what’s known as a :Despite dealing with a sore shoulder, Hart picked Harden’s pocket twice, converting one steal into a layup. Unfortunately, after Bridges tied the game at 55, Donovan Mitchell (30 PTS, 1-7 3PT) and Harden combined for six unanswered points, aided by a Bridges turnover. The home team won the quarter 33-27 but entered intermission trailing 61-56.Through the half, Harden and Mitchell combined for 34 points in the half, while their bench contributed 13. New York had shot better from the field (54% to 49%) and significantly better from deep (50% to 31%), they were on the wrong end of the score due to a glaring free-throw disparity. New York had attempted just eight freebies, while Cleveland shot more than twice that. The Cavs outscored won the paint, 28-16, and the boards. Another glaring stat: Cleveland converted six Knicks miscues into 13 points, while New York squeezed just two points out of five giveaways.Cleveland opened the second half on an 11-5 run to restore its double-digit lead. Down 74-65 midway through the period, the Knicks got a boost from an unexpected source: Tyler Nickel. The rookie sank a triple, followed by another from Landry Shamet, to cut the deficit to three. Nickel contributed five points but also committed four fouls in under six minutes—that will get straightened out with experience. Harden extended Cleveland’s advantage to 85-77 with under three minutes remaining. But then another unexpected player pitched in: James Wiseman provided some valuable minutes off the bench, finishing the game with six points and seven boards in six minutes. Shamet helped the Knicks win the quarter 26-24 and enter the fourth trailing 85-82.The Knicks opened the fourth quarter on a 12-0 run, turning a three-point deficit into a nine-point advantage in less than three minutes. Jose Alvarado (a team-high 21 points, 8-10 FG, 19 MIN) was the catalyst, drilling consecutive triples and picking Donovan Mitchell’s pocket to set up a Dadiet layup. Hart took a turn orchestrating the offense, collecting four assists during the opening surge. The Ohio Players missed their first five shots, four of them by Mitchell, and committed two turnovers as the Knicks piled on the points.Wiseman (!) helped goose New York’s lead to 13 with four points and three offensive rebounds in a brief fourth-quarter stint. When Mitchell and Harden scored five unanswered points to trim the deficit to eight, Alvarado responded with a jumper, and Jalen Brunson buried a triple, his only basket of the quarter. Alvarado was the unquestionable star of the fourth, scoring 16 of his 21 points, including four three-pointers. Hart was nearly as impactful, contributing eight points, six assists, three rebounds, a steal, and a block in the frame. The Knicks closed on a 7-0 run, their defense holding Cleveland scoreless over the final two minutes and change.Welcome back to associate head coach Chris Jent, who returned to the sidelines after a month away.The Knicks hang around town to face the Heat on Friday in the last of their first-stage Cup games. Mo is folding and pressing your recap. Happy Knicksgiving, turkey fans.

item.title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
item.author: Stephen Clark
item.content:encoded: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.

item.title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
item.author: Samuel Axon
item.content:encoded: Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi's blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

item.title: Backblaze explains why it's sharing customer information with advertisers
item.author: Scharon Harding
item.content:encoded: Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze's privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.”The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.

item.title: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites

item.content:encoded: In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold."The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth."

item.title: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
item.author: Nick Indge
item.content:encoded: Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it's an installable package with automatic updating.Ladybird is most notable for what it isn't: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google's Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird's rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. "The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork," project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday's announcement. "The browser around it is modest, but functional."

item.title: Etsy clarifies AI terms after seller backlash
item.author: Cyrus Farivar
item.content:encoded: After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the company to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the company's terms of service and admitted that her team "should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content."“Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we're using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”

item.title: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop
item.author: Jeremy Hsu
item.content:encoded:
Drone attacks on data centers.
Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there's an incentive to target it.

item.title: 'The more I was thinking, the more I didn't know what to do' – Primož Roglič on looking retirement in the eye, his 'really fast' move to NSN, and why he could even race beyond 2027
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: Primož Roglič looked retirement square in the eye this off-season. He didn’t mind what he saw, but there was a definite itch as he pictured his career in that hypothetical rear-view mirror. "You have two sides," he explained, speaking at his new team's first pre-season training camp. "If you want to finish when you can choose, you want to finish while you are still good, or on the top. "The other is that I'm still attracted by cycling, you know. I like it. I like to compete, I still have unfinished businesses with it... [so that] I can peacefully say at the end of my cycling career that that was it."Roglič went on to describe the sort of situation in which it would make no sense for him to carry on: "That you don't care, if it's first place, 10th place, 100th place – just that it doesn't touch you anymore and you are done with it."That’s clearly not the case for the 37-year-old champion of five Grand Tours. And not just that, but 2027 is not necessarily the end, either. Roglič’s has joined NSN on a one-year contract that was billed by the team themselves as 'the final chapter'. However, he is not ruling out continuing his career into 2028."You know, how to say it… the only fixed thing in life…" he said, perhaps referring to the saying that the only two certainties in life are death and taxes."We start with this one [season]. In the minute it’s the final one, but let’s start and we see how we go, and where we go."Roglič was then asked about the possible Tour de France Grand Départ in his native Slovenia in 2029. "Now it’s 2027. In 2029 I will be 40," he joked. He did go on to say "maybe", but, as the journalist in question revealed he himself was 40, he was clearly in tongue-in-cheek mode: "Ah you look good. Yeah, Maybe, maybe, if I look like this, then yeah."Roglič’s move to NSN, announced last Wednesday, was a sudden and surprising end to a transfer saga that had rumbled on for much of the season. It was clear by the summer that the four-time Vuelta a España winner would not be continuing at Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and he didn’t appear to be awash with options, with Lotto-Intermarché, Tudor Pro Cycling and Pinarello-Q36.5 being the strongest links. The uncertainty rumbled on right through to his last race of the season, Il Lombardia, where he told us he might just be about to race his final race. He had offers on the table but he had a more pressing concern: whether or not he even wanted to carry on. "It took a while, definitely, for me to figure it out, after the season – what to do, in which direction to go," Roglič said."Then I started thinking, and the more I was thinking, the more I didn't know actually what to do."So in the end, I really needed to let it go, you know, to look from a bit of a different perspective at some things."Roglič stated that the fundamental decision over retirement came first, and then made way for the more practical considerations of what another season could look like. "First of all, it was more about continuing racing or not. And yes, then, okay, this was done. But then still it was open – how to continue, where to continue. "When I'd figured it out, I mean, what actually would count the most for me? What would be something new, something different?"In the end, I came to the things, or the basics, that I would appreciate the most. So that was trust, belief, and support from the team and all the rest around the equipment and whatever that follows into this."A lightning fast move to NSNRoglič firmly felt he found those things with NSN Cycling, the team formerly known as Israel-Premier Tech that in 2026 turned into the Swiss-registered outfit that’s now operated by ex-footballer Andres Iniesta’s ‘Never Say Never’ company. NSN, who had little in the way of climbing or GC depth but now have Roglič and Richard Carapaz on the books, weren’t in the mix until very recently. In fact, Roglič had solid offers in his hand at the time he was mulling his retirement, but contact with NSN only came very late, and accelerated very quickly. It was less than two weeks ago, he says, that he and his agent sat down with the team’s representatives, including general manager Kjell Carlstrom, sporting manager Steve Bauer, and head sports director Sam Bewley. "I mean, first of all, they listened, you know, they listened," Roglič said pointedly. "And when they spoke, I got the feeling that they are the ones that I can get full trust in, that I will get full support and belief. So with that kind of feelings, it was pretty fast."A few days later, he had put pen to paper, and a few days after that, he arrived in south east Spain at the team’s first pre-season training camp. And a few days on again, he's talking to us. "It was really fast and easy, and I'm happy that I got this opportunity, and I'm really happy that I'm here now," Roglič said."Let's say I didn't care, and I started to discover… I started to, yeah, to be actually positively surprised since I came last Saturday here to the team camp."Roglič did not map out his 2027 calendar, saying that all three Grand Tours were enticing in their own way but that it was “too early” to be thinking about that, adding: "it’s unfair now to do this, because now I try to meet here 150 people, I don’t know much about the equipment. First things first."More generally, though, he knows he has to take care of that unfinished business. This autumn he came agonisingly close to an outright-record fifth Vuelta title, and went on to win the European time trial title. They wouldn't have been a shabby set of results to bow out on, and they would in fact take some beating in 2027, but it's more the idea of going out on his own terms. "I hope something good," Roglič said of what he hopes to get out of 2027. "Everyone likes things to happen, if you say victories or whatever, but the only sure thing is challenges. The challenges will come. You know, the shit things will come. That is something that is pretty sure, and that actually I'm looking forward to – to dealing with it. "Hopefully I still can give, in terms of results, definitely something good back, and that we are all happy, you know, with giving our best this year." The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Landry Shamet has arrived. Why can’t he be Sixth Man of the Year?
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: Chicken Littles can relax. Our world champion Knicks are 11–6, sit fourth in the Eastern Conference, and have won eight of their last 10 games, including five straight. Karl-Anthony Towns is having an MVP-caliber season, and Captain Jalen Brunson is warming up after a short, celebration-heavy offseason. Another player who’s getting some buzz isn’t one of the starters, but the team’s sharpest weapon off the bench.When asked about Landry Shamet’s play this season, head coach Mike Brown said the 6’5” guard “should be Sixth Man of the Year. It’s not close.” Mike should know. He has a front-row seat to the Shamet show every night and at every practice.One stat I take note of is Game Score. John Hollinger designed it to measure a player’s box-score production in a single game. Game Score uses a scale that roughly resembles points scored, with 10 considered an average performance and 40 an outstanding one. It rewards scoring, made field goals, rebounds, assists, steals, and blocks. Shot attempts, missed free throws, turnovers, and personal fouls subtract from the total, and offensive rebounds count more than defensive rebounds.Through 17 games, Shamet has averaged a Game Score of 8.24. That puts him fourth on the team behind Towns (19.83), Brunson (18.66), and OG Anunoby (11.57). Two starters, Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges, rank fifth and sixth at 6.35 and 5.94, respectively.This season has been a coming out party for Landry. Although primarily a linchpin of the second unit, he has filled in for starters five times this campaign and is averaging 26.9 minutes per game, the second-most of his NBA career. Consider these statistics, all career-best:A shade under 50% from the field65% effective field goal percentageEight field goal attempts per game5.6 triples tried per game11.4 points per game, fourth-best on the teamThe only Knick shooting better from deep is Jordan Clarkson (50%), coincidentally the 2020–21 Sixth Man of the Year. And Jordan’s attempted only 12 longballs.When Hart and Bridges have struggled to find the net, plenty of people have beaten the drum for Shamet to replace one of them in the first five. That sounds fine in theory, but consider Mike Brown’s perspective. First, there’s the harmony of keeping the Villanova brethren together, and who knows what effect a “demotion” for Josh or Kal might have on the locker room? Second, Shamet is Mike’s security blanket. If the starters are spinning their wheels, nothing injects energy into the festivities like a Landry pull-up three on the move. The MSG crowd explodes, and you can see his teammates quicken with excitement. Furthermore, Shamet is doing much of his damage against the opponent’s backups. That’s hardly a fair fight. AND when the score is close and the team needs a bucket, Brown can turn to Captain Clutch, Towns, and his sparkplug Shamet. Even if Landry doesn’t start, he sure can finish.One downer about Landry’s success is the ripple effect on the roster. Overshadowed by Shamet’s sizzling shooting is the fact that Miles McBride is also shooting a career high from downtown (42%). Deuce was once a first-off-the-bench candidate. Now, with Shamet hitting the three-ball and Tyler Kolek coming into his own as a playmaker (averaging 4.1 assists to 0.6 turnovers in 13.3 minutes per game), McBride is down to 17.2 minutes per night, the fourth-highest average of his six-season career. Meanwhile, the Knicks find themselves dreadfully thin at center, with Andre Drummond losing the plot around the 10-minute mark most nights and James Wiseman yet to prove he can hang. Shamet + Kolek + Drummond + Wiseman = an expendable Deuce. No one here will be surprised if McBride, the longest-tenured Knick, is traded before the deadline for a serviceable big man. No, we won’t like it, but we’ll understand it.Consider this: only three Knicks have won Sixth Man of the Year.Why can’t ShamWow be the fourth? He’ll have some stiff competition in the race. Boston’s Payton Pritchard is the current betting favorite for Sixth Man of the Year (+160 at BetMGM). That vanilla Milk Dud averages 13.7 points per game. Other top contenders include Ajay Mitchell (Thunder), Dylan Harper (Spurs), Jrue Holiday (Blazers), and Ayo Dosunmu (Timberwolves). Jared McCain and Daniss Jenkins are dark horses.The stats make Landry a strong candidate, though. Through Nov. 22, Shamet ranked fifth in the NBA in on/off net rating among 242 qualifying players on HoopsNightly’s leaderboard. The Knicks outscored opponents by 17.2 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor and were outscored by 8.3 with him off it. That’s a swing of +25.5. (KnickStats gives him an even better number, +28.)There used to be two knocks on Shamet, now in his ninth season. The first was that his defense stunk. Well, whattayaknow: according to KnickStats, the Knicks have allowed 101.3 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor and 117.5 with him off it. The other concern was the injury bug. He’s missed significant time with lower-body issues, including multiple ankle sprains, a foot injury that kept him out for an extended stretch in 2023, and a calf strain that ended his 2023–24 season. Then came the right-shoulder setbacks, a dislocation in the 2024 preseason and a sprain in 2025 that sidelined him for roughly a month. For now (no jinxes), he’s been the picture of health, playing every game of the campaign (we all wince whenever he smashes to the floor).Everything’s good until it isn’t again. So it goes. For now, the Knicks are surging and tonight they’ll face a familiar rival in the Cleveland Cavaliers. If you saw the injury report, it’s a little dicey. Anunoby and Clarkson are out, while Hart, McBride, and Towns are all game-time decisions. That’s a concerning list at first blush, but with sixth man Shamet in their back pocket, the Knicks still have a good chance to win their sixth straight. What a time to be a fan.

item.title: The UCI's registration rules strike again, delaying Shirin van Anrooij's debut with Canyon-SRAM
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Now, the Dutch rider will have to don a plain jersey for the first five weeks of her off-road season, Canyon-SRAM announced on Instagram."Since joining Canyon-SRAM on Nov. 1, @shirnivananrooij has settled nicely into the team & familiarised herself with new equipment. In accordance with UCI regulations, she'll be registered independently & compete in non-team kit for cyclo-cross races from Nov. 27 until Jan. 1," the team wrote.Van Anrooij is due to race alongside new teammate Zoe Backstedt in the first round of the UCI World Cup in Ostrava on Friday and another dozen races, culminating with the UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships at the end of January.However, because her transfer from Lidl-Trek to Canyon-SRAM was not completed in the UCI's mid-season transfer window of August 1-15, her registration with her new team cannot officially take effect until January 1.Van Anrooij could have been racing in the Canyon-SRAM kit had the team registered a cyclo-cross team separately. Blanka Vas will be racing cyclocross with Lidl-Trek after leaving SD Worx-ProTime.Registration rules have long plagued professional cycling, resulting in incoming riders being put in the awkward position of wearing plain kits during teams' December training camps, and hiding photo shoots in their new kit under lock and key until the dawn of the new year.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl
item.author: Beth Mole
item.content:encoded: In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate.Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast.
